newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Stock market bulls set to run and run in Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: Stock market bulls set to run and run in Taiwan.

text.p: A recovering economy and solid government backing have helped drive Taiwan's main share index more than 400 points higher this month and analysts said the bulls had yet to run their course despite Tuesday's slight dip.
The weighted index slipped 11.10 points on Tuesday to 6,927.77 on hectic turnover of T$104.37 billion as profit-takers cashed in after the recent rises.
The index has risen 342 points in seven sessions.
"Many investors decided to slow their pace after the big recent gains," said Foremost Investment analyst Norman Lee.
The bull run started last week with what brokers called politically motivated, state-linked buying, marking six months since President Lee Teng-hui's May 20 inauguration.
Adding to the upbeat mood was an announcement by the Securities and Exchange Commission easing the upper limit on foreign ownership of Taiwan equity to 25 percent from 20 percent.
It also raised the ceiling on single foreign investments in any one listed company to 10 percent from 7.5 percent.
Oliver Fang, a manager at National Securities, said the government-orchestrated rally had not lost its steam.
"The market just needs a break. The bull run is far from finishing," he said, adding that the index would likely top 7,200 this year.
"It is obvious the government is backing the market. A bull run with government's support will not be short-lived."
An expected rebound in the economy and plentiful liquidity would also fuel the market's growth, analysts said.
The government's statistics bureau has predicted fourth-quarter gross domestic product will grow a year-on-year 6.6 percent, almost a percentage point higher than the third-quarter's 5.61 percent.
Interest rate cuts had also driven savings investors to stocks, brokers said.
"Money seems to be coming from everywhere," Fang said. "Market liquidity is abundant and everyone is so bullish."
Most brokers expected the market to beat a retreat on a technical correction but to recover to test the 7,000-point barrier this year.

Nikko Securities expects the index to test 8,600 in 1997 and rachet towards 10,000 in 1998, boosted in part by bullish "greater China" sentiment after the British colony of Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule next year.

Removal of final political obstacles to direct shipping between Taiwan and China after five decades of estrangement would also help fuel China-Taiwan-Hong Kong business and, in turn, higher Taiwan share prices, brokers said.
